paragraphs.text: The prophet being thus called and confirmed, {as Jer 1:1-19} sets forthwith upon the work. Est autem hoc caput plenum querelae, et quasi continuum pathos. In this chapter the Lord heavily complaineth of Jerusalem’s unworthy usage of him, convincing them thereof by sixteen different arguments, as A Lapide hath observed; and all little enough; for they put him to his proofs, as is to be seen. {Jer 2:35}
paragraphs.anchor: Moreover, the word of the Lord came to me, saying.

paragraphs.text: For if I myself should do it immediately from heaven, my stillest rhetoric would be too loud for them. {Deu 5:27-28}
paragraphs.anchor: Go thou and cry.

paragraphs.text: Who hast forgot thy first love and loyalty to me. Or, "I remember," that is, I put thee in mind of the kindness that hath been between us. Augustus might have some such meaning in those last words of his to his wife when he lay a dying, ‘O Livia, remember our marriage, and adieu.’ It is thought she had a hand in setting him going, and that she was too familiar with Eudemus the physician. Qui specie artis frequens secretis, saith Tacitus. Peccatum est deicidium.
paragraphs.anchor: I remember thee.

paragraphs.text: When thou camest out of Egypt after me, and wast espoused unto me at the giving of the law. We use highly to prize nettle buds when they first put forth, so doth God our young services. Others render it thus: I record the mercy showed to thee in thy youth, and the love of thy espousals - sc., whenas I loved thee because I loved thee, and for no other reason. {Deu 7:7-8}
paragraphs.anchor: The kindness of thy youth.

paragraphs.text: God takes it kindly when men will choose him, and his ways in affliction, as did Moses. {Heb 11:25} "Who is this that cometh from the wilderness" - from troubles and afflictions - "leaning on her beloved?" {Son 8:5}
paragraphs.anchor: When thou wentest after me in the wilderness.

paragraphs.text: A people consecrated and set apart for his peculiar; {Exo 19:5 Psa 114:2} holy with a federal holiness at least.
paragraphs.anchor: Israel was holiness unto the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Yea, his "firstborn," and therefore, "higher than the kings of the earth." {Psa 89:27} All God’s people are so. {Heb 12:23 Jas 1:18}
paragraphs.anchor: And the firstfruits of his increase.

paragraphs.text: Rather thus: All that devoured them trespassed - evil befell them; witness the four latter books of Moses.
paragraphs.anchor: All that devour them shall offend.

paragraphs.text: This is often inculcated in both Testaments, to procure attention. "I received of the Lord, that which also I delivered unto you." {1Co 11:23} "This we say unto you by the word of the Lord." {1Th 4:15} Thus to preach, is to preach cum privilegio, with authority.
paragraphs.anchor: Hear ye the word of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: How unreasonable was their apostasy! and how senseless is your pleading from their example! Nothing is more irrational than irreligion.
paragraphs.anchor: What iniquity have your fathers found in me?

paragraphs.text: Are ye weary of receiving so many benefits by one man? said Themistocles to his ungrateful countrymen.
paragraphs.anchor: That they are gone far from me.

paragraphs.text: An idol is nothing at all, but only in the vain opinion of the idolater.
paragraphs.anchor: And have walked after vanity.

paragraphs.text: scil., " In their imaginations"; {Rom 1:21} as vain as their very idols. {Psa 115:8}
paragraphs.anchor: And are become vain

paragraphs.text: In their minds, or with their mouths. That signal deliverance was obliterated, and even lost upon them. Plerique omnes sumus ingrati. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Neither said they.

paragraphs.text: Per terrain campestrem et sepulchralem, where we talked of making our graves; neither was it any otherwise likely, but that God gave us pluviam escatilem et petram aquatilem, {b} all manner of necessaries.
paragraphs.anchor: Through a land of deserts and of pits.

paragraphs.text: {a} Cicero.
{b} Tertul.

You lived in my good land, but not by my good laws; you had aequissima iura, sed iniquissima ingenia, most just laws but most foul nature, as was said of the Athenians; as if I had hired you to be wicked, so have you abused my mercies to my greatest dishonour.
paragraphs.anchor: And I brought you into a plentiful country.

paragraphs.text: The priests said not, {a} Where is the Lord?] Ignorant they were, and idle. They would not be at the pains of a serious inquisition after God and his will; though he be a "rewarder of all that diligently seek him." {Heb 11:6}
That expounded and applied it. A metaphor from such as are trained in the war, who are said tractate bellum, to handle their arms.
paragraphs.anchor: And they that handled the law.

paragraphs.text: What marvel, therefore, that the people did so too? For, as in a fish, the corruption of it beginneth at the head; so here.
paragraphs.anchor: The pastors also transgressed against me.

paragraphs.text: And taught others to worship idols. We see then, it is nothing new that stars fall from heaven, that church chieftains should fall from God, and draw others after them. It went for a proverb, a little before Luther stirred, Qui theologum seholasticum videt, videt septem peccata mortalia, He that seeth a divine, seeth the seven deadly sins.
paragraphs.anchor: And the prophets prophesied by Baal.

paragraphs.text: {a} Dixerunt, Ubi victimae, ubi nummi? triobolarium Deum faciunt subque hastam mittunt. - Oecol.
i.e., Debate the case with you, and set you down by sound reason. So he did to our first parents when they had sinned; but doomed the serpent without any more ado.
paragraphs.anchor: I will yet plead with you

paragraphs.text: The western parts of the world - Greece, Italy, Cyprus, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: For pass over the isles of Chittim.

paragraphs.text: The eastern parts, where dwell Kedarens, Arabians, Saracens, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: And send unto Kedar.

paragraphs.text: No; they are too pertinacious in their superstitions. Xenophon saith it was an oracle of Apollo, that those gods are rightly worshipped which were delivered them by their ancestors; and this he greatly applaudeth. Cicero also saith, that no reason shall ever prevail with him to relinquish the religion of his forefathers. That monarch of Morocco told an English ambassador, that he had lately read St Paul, and that he disliked nothing in him but this, that he had changed his religion. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Hath a nation changed their gods?

paragraphs.text: Sed hominum figmenta et ludibria daemonum. But are the invention of men and mockery of demons. When Hercules came into a temple, and found the image or statue of Adonis in it, he pulled it down with this expression, Certe nil sacri es, Sure thou art no god; the like may be said of all idols.
paragraphs.anchor: Which yet are no gods.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Their God, of whom they might glory, saying, {as Deu 32:31} "Their rock is not as our rock, our enemies themselves being judges."
paragraphs.anchor: But my people have changed their glory

paragraphs.text: {a} Heyl., Cosmography.
A poetic and pathetic expression. Compare Deu 32:1 Isa 1:2.
paragraphs.anchor: Be astonished, O heavens!

paragraphs.text: Horripilamini portento malitiae, quod iam dicturus sum; be aghast at such a prodigious wickedness.
paragraphs.anchor: Be horribly afraid.

paragraphs.text: As the sun seemed to be, when at the death of Christ he hid his head in a mantle of black, which made, they say, {a} the heathen astrologer break out into these words, Either the God of nature suffereth, or else the world is at an end.
paragraphs.anchor: Be very desolate.

paragraphs.text: {a} Dionys.

Contrary to those two good things that I have commanded them, viz., "Depart from evil, and do good." {Psa 34:14} Lust doth first εξελκειν, draw a man from God, and then it doth δελεαζειν, deceive him with a bait of the creature. {Jas 1:14}
paragraphs.anchor: For my people have committed two evils.

paragraphs.text: The all-sufficient, ever-flowing, over-flowing well spring of all welfare. {Jas 1:17} Trismegist, a heathen, could say, {a} Respicite O mortales, et resipiscite, et ad fontem vitae recurrite, Look back, O mortals, and repent, and run back again to the fountain of life. Seneca also saith, that sin is so foul a thing, that he would not commit it, though he could hide it from men, and get pardon of it of God; for that were to turn his back upon God, the chief good, &c. How well might Bullinger {b} say, that Seneca alone had left to posterity more sincere divinity than all the books of almost all the schoolmen.
paragraphs.anchor: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.

paragraphs.text: Such, and no better, are all idols, human helps, creature comforts, friends, means, merits, &c.; what are they all but cisterns, that hold but muddy rainwater at best? but then, being broken cisterns, riven vessels, what hold they else but limum et lapides, mud and gravel? Such cisterns, therefore, to hew out, what is it better than industrious folly, laborious loss of time? to say no worse of it. Now
paragraphs.anchor: And hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns.

paragraphs.text: “ Turpe est difficiles habere nugas:
Et stultus labor est ineptiarum. ”
{a} Dialog. 7.
{b} Comment. in Rom 1:19. So little reason was there that Alex. Hales should be called first Fons vitae, font of life, and then Doctor Irrefragabilis, irresistible teacher.
sc., Bought with money. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Is Israel a servant?

paragraphs.text: Verna, a slave by birth; q.d., if he be either of the two, he may thank himself. He was my son, nay, my spouse, if he could have kept him so; but he hath sold himself to commit wickedness, and I have therefore sold him into the hands of the Chaldeans. Lo! this is the product of his forsaking me, the fountain of living waters, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Is he a homeborn slave?

paragraphs.text: {a} Servus empticius, purchased slave.

i.e., The King of Babylon and his forces, more fierce and fell than young lions. Would any take the Church’s picture? saith Luther; {a} then let him paint a silly, poor maid, sitting in a wood or wilderness, compassed about with hungry lions, wolves, boars, and bears; for this is her condition in the world.
paragraphs.anchor: The young lions roared upon him, and yelled

paragraphs.text: i.e., They shall shortly so make it.
paragraphs.anchor: And they made his land waste

paragraphs.text: {a} Loc. com. tit. de persecut. verae Ecclesia.

Two chief cities of Egypt, the inhabitants whereof were said to be most effeminate and servile fellows; {a} even these shall overtop thee, knock thee down, as an ox by a blow on the brain pan, and make havoc of those things that thou holdest the chiefest and most desirable.
paragraphs.anchor: Also the children of Noph and Tahapanes.

paragraphs.text: {a} Herodot., lib. ii.

The same may the Lord say to every sufferer: and further add, "Did not I warn you, saying, Sin not against the child?" {Gen 42:22} Oh, do not this abominable thing! your iniquities will undoubtedly be your ruin, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Hast thou not procured this to thyself?

paragraphs.text: The way that is called holy, the highway to heaven; fitly here opposed to those byways of carnal wisdom, mentioned in the following verses.
paragraphs.anchor: When he led thee by the way.

paragraphs.text: Why trusteth thou to carnal combinations, which thou hast formerly found to lack in success? wilt thou never be warned of these broken cisterns? or hast thou a mind to be ground to powder between those two millstones of Egypt and Assyria, after whom thou hankerest? Psa 146:3, David having entered a caveat against creature confidence, persuades people to trust in God alone. See also Psa 62:8-10.
paragraphs.anchor: And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt?

paragraphs.text: i.e., Of Nile, called Sihor, of its blackness or muddiness; {a} and in Greek, Mελας, black. To drink the waters of it here is to draw the Egyptian forces to thine assistance, and, as some think, to partake with them in their superstitions.
paragraphs.anchor: To drink the waters of Sihor

paragraphs.text: i.e., Of Euphrates, that river by an eminence.
paragraphs.anchor: To drink of the water of the river

paragraphs.text: {a} Limosus est Nilus et oblimat Aegyptum.

Erudiat te malitia tua; let thine own wickedness, with the sad consequents thereof, teach thee better things. {as Jer 6:8} Let it for shame, let it παθων δε τε νηποις εγνω, let smart make wit. {Isa 28:19 Pro 29:15}
paragraphs.anchor: Thine own wickedness shall correct thee.

paragraphs.text: Learn at least by sad experience, for thou hast paid for thy learning. Piscator ictus sapiet.
paragraphs.anchor: Know therefore, and see.

paragraphs.text: So all sin will prove in the issue, and when the bottom of the bag is turned upward. There will be "bitterness in the end," as Abner said to Joab. {2Sa 2:26} Laban will show himself at parting howsoever. Tamar will be more hated than ever she was loved: Amor, amarior; plus aloes quam mellis habet.
paragraphs.anchor: That it is an evil thing and bitter.

paragraphs.text: “ Laeta venire Venus, tristis abire solet. ”

Drunkenness is sweet, but wormwood is bitter. These inhabitants of Jerusalem were made drunk, but with wormwood; {Lam 3:15} they found that sin was a Dulc-acldum, {a} a bitter sweet - sweet in the mouth, but bitter in the maw, {stomach} as that book in the Revelation; like Adam’s apple, or Esau’s pottage, or Jonathan’s honey, or Judas’s thirty pieces, whereof he would fain have been rid, but could not; they burned like a spark of hell fire in his hand, but especially in his conscience. The devil, with the panther, hideth his deformed head till the sweet scent have drawn other beasts into his danger, and then he devoureth them. Did we but consider what sin will cost us at last, we dare not but be innocent.
{a} γλυκυπικρον. - Philo.
Or, For when of old I broke thy yoke, &c. - sc., in Egypt; {Psa 81:5-6; Psa 81:10} while the deliverance was fresh, thou hadst very good resolutions.
paragraphs.anchor: For of old time I have broken thy yoke.

paragraphs.text: Or, I will not serve, sc., other gods. Good words, hadst thou been as good as thy word. But what followeth?
paragraphs.anchor: And thou saidst, I will not transgress.

paragraphs.text: No sooner did her old heart and her old temptations meet, but they presently fell into mutual embraces. When men have made good vows, let them be as careful to make good their vows unto the Lord. {Psa 76:11}
paragraphs.anchor: When upon every high hill, and under every green tree, &c.

paragraphs.text: Thou runnest to madding and gadding after idols, ειδωλομανης.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou wanderest, playing the harlot.

paragraphs.text: Heb., A sorek, or with slips of sorek. {Jdg 16:4} See Isa 5:3, a parallel text; Exo 15:17 Psa 44:3; Psa 80:9.
paragraphs.anchor: Ver 21. Yet I had planted thee a noble vine.

paragraphs.text: That should have yielded a right crop, but it proveth otherwise. Nec votis respondet avari agricolae.
paragraphs.anchor: Wholly a right seed.

paragraphs.text: How is it that slips of sorek prove slips of Sodom? {Deu 32:32} See on Isa 5:4; Isa 5:7.
paragraphs.anchor: How then art thou turned into the degenerate plant?

paragraphs.text: Much used of old by fullers and neat laundresses, say Isidore and Athanasius, {a} now not known in these parts; apothecaries use saltpetre instead of it. Sin leaveth behind it a deep stain, so ingrained that it will hardly ever be gotten out, not at all by blanching, extenuating, excusing, &c., or by any legal purifications, hypocritical lotions. All which notwithstanding,
paragraphs.anchor: For though thou wash thee with nitre.

paragraphs.text: Nitet iniquitas tua, splendet instar auri, {b} It glisters like gold before me, whose eyes thou canst not blind or blear with any of thy colourable pretexts and pretences.
paragraphs.anchor: Thine iniquity is marked before me.

paragraphs.text: {a} Lib. xvi. Etym.; Lib. de Virg. - Nitrum sordes erodit et expurgat. - Plin.
{b} Piscat.
q.d., With what face? but that sin hath woaded an impudence in thy face.
paragraphs.anchor: How canst thou say, I am not polluted?

paragraphs.text: The whole crew of heathen deities - lords or masters, the word signifieth - which Cicero {a} saith were but men; their temples were their sepulchres, and their religion superstition. He further wisheth that he could as easily discern the true religion as discover the false.
paragraphs.anchor: I have not gone after Baalim.

paragraphs.text: Of Ben-Hinnom, where thou hast sacrificed thy children to Moloch, thy chief Baal - that is, say some, to the sun, as to the universal cause, strongly concurring to the generation of their children so sacrificed. {b}
paragraphs.anchor: See thy way in the valley.

paragraphs.text: That runneth amadding after her mate; so dost thou after idols. Compare 1Co 12:2.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art a swift dromedary.

paragraphs.text: {a} De Nat. Deor.
{b} Sol et homo generant hominem.
Untameable and untractable, {Job 39:8} especially when proud and in the heat of lust, as these were after their idols.
paragraphs.anchor: A wild ass used to the wilderness.

paragraphs.text: When she windeth the male; so this people when acted by a spirit of fornications.
paragraphs.anchor: That snuffeth up the wind.

paragraphs.text: i.e., In her last month, when she is so big with young that she cannot wield herself. So sinners, be they never so stubborn, so stiff and high in the instep, that there is no dealing with them, yet when they are in straits and distresses it will be otherwise. God, said Mr Marbury, is fain to deal with wicked men, as men do with frisking jades in a pasture, that cannot be taken up till gotten to a gate; so till he seize upon them by some judgment or summons to die, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: In her month they shall find her

paragraphs.text: Cease thy vain vagaries to the wearing out of thy shoes, and exposing thyself to extreme thirst; or rather take a timely course to prevent captivity, and the miseries that attend it. {Isa 20:2; Isa 20:4; Isa 47:2}
paragraphs.anchor: Withhold thy foot from being unshod, &c.

paragraphs.text: viz., Of reclaiming us; we are resolved on our course, and will take our swing in sin whatsoever come of it. {Isa 28:14-15; Isa 57:10} Some grow desperately sinful, saith a reverend modern writer, {a} like those Italian senators that, despairing of their lives, when upon submission they had been promised their lives, yet being conscious of their villany made a curious banquet, and at the end thereof, every man drank up his glass of poison and killed himself; so men, feeling such horrible hard hearts, and privy to such notorious sins, they cast away souls and all for lust, and so perish woefully, because they lived desperately and so securely.
paragraphs.anchor: But thou saidst, There is no hope

paragraphs.text: {a} Mr Shepherd’s Sincere Convert, 222.

As usually he is at length, notwithstanding all his sleights and wiles. That was a cunning thief indeed of whom Dio writeth in the life of Severus. Bulas he calleth him, an Italian, who having gotten together six hundred such as himself, robbed many in Italy under the emperor’s nose for two years together; and although he was diligently sought for by the emperor and his armies, yet he could not be caught. Visis enim non videbatur, non inveniebatur inventus, deprehensus non capiebatur, saith the historian; he was too hard for them all.
paragraphs.anchor: As the thief is ashamed when he is found.

paragraphs.text: They are, or ought to be so; but
paragraphs.anchor: So is the house of Israel ashamed.

paragraphs.text: “ Nihil est audacius illis
Deprensis: vires animosque a crimine sumunt. ”

i.e., My God. {Isa 44:17} We are not the children of fornication, said those boasting Jews; {Joh 8:41} that is, we are not idolaters, who say, as here, to a stock, Thou art my father. The Samaritans they called bastards.
paragraphs.anchor: Saying to a stock, Thou art my father

paragraphs.text: Thus in their month they will be found. {Jer 2:24} When they had run themselves barefoot in following their lovers, {Jer 2:25} who answered their expectation with nothing but fear, and sent them away with shame instead of glory, then God was thought upon and sought unto. Let us make God our choice, and not our necessity, and labour to maintain such constant cause with him, that he may know our souls in adversity, and not turn us off, as he doth these, with,
paragraphs.anchor: But in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us.

paragraphs.text: Thou hast sure no need of my help. Quasi tu huius indigeas patris. See the like, Jdg 10:14. {See Trapp on "Jdg 10:14"}
paragraphs.anchor: But where are thy gods that thou hast made thee?

paragraphs.text: Enough of them thou hast, and near enough. The Papists also have their tutelar saints, to whom they seek more than to God himself. And when the Ave Mary bell rings, which is at sunrise, noon, and sunset, all men, in whatever place, house, field, street, or market, do presently kneel down and send up their united devotions to heaven by an Ave Maria. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: For according to the number of thy cities are thy gods.

paragraphs.text: {a} Spec. Europ.
Putting me to my proofs. Is not the case clear enough? Will ye not yield to reason? See on Jer 2:19.
paragraphs.anchor: Wherefore will ye plead with me?

paragraphs.text: And yet ye have the face to ask, as in Jer 16:10, "What is our iniquity, or what is our sin that we have committed against the Lord?" And to say, as in Hos 12:8, "In all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me: that were sin." See there.
paragraphs.anchor: Ye all have transgressed against me.

paragraphs.text: My hammers have but beaten cold iron; ye are incorrigible, irreformable. See Isa 1:5. {See Trapp on "Isa 1:5"}
paragraphs.anchor: In vain have I smitten your children.

paragraphs.text: As it did in the days of Ahaz, Joash, Manasseh, of whom Josephus {a} saith, that he slew some prophet of God every day.
paragraphs.anchor: Your own sword hath devoured your prophets.

paragraphs.text: Cum saevitia summa, exuta omni humanitate. Ye have pulled them limb meal, and caused them to die piece meal.
paragraphs.anchor: Like a destroying lion.

paragraphs.text: {a} Lib. x. cap. 4.

q.d., O generation, rather leonine than human! as Jer 2:30. "See ye the word"; I say not to you, Hear; no more than I would to a savage beast; for ye have no ears to hear reason; but see with your eyes, for so even beasts can do. See now, and say sooth.
paragraphs.anchor: O generation, see ye the word of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Such as is described before. {Jer 2:6} Or, Have I not rather been a paradise unto you, and a storehouse of all accommodations and comforts? It well appeareth that they have wanted nothing but thankful hearts, by this, that fulness hath bred forgetfulness; for so stout they are grown by reason of their great wealth, that they will not come at me, nor acknowledge my sovereignty over them, but will needs be petty gods within themselves. We are lords, say they, and will not now take it as we have done. The ancient Greek rendereth it, We will not be ruled.
paragraphs.anchor: Have I been a wilderness unto Israel?

paragraphs.text: Not lightly or easily, as minding them many times more than is meet, and then their ornaments are but the nest of pride; and while they think to gain more credit by their garments than by their graces, they are much mistaken.
paragraphs.anchor: Can a maid forget her ornaments?

paragraphs.text: i.e., Time out of mind, whenas God should be remembered at every breath we draw, since from him we have ζωην και πνοην, "life and breath," as the apostle saith elegantly. {Act 17:25} But into such a dead lethargy hath sin cast most people, that God is forgotten by them, and his service neglected.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet my people have forgotten me, days without number

paragraphs.text: Cur bonificas? so Calvin rendereth it why dost thou make good thy way? that is, set a good gloss upon it, even the best side outwards. The same word is used of Jezebel’s dressing her head. {2Ki 9:30} What need this whorish trick and trimming, if all were right with thee?
paragraphs.anchor: Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love?

paragraphs.text: “ Iactas vaenales, quas vis obtrudere, merces. ”

Heb., The wicked women - for the word is feminine - those she-sinners may learn immodesty of thee, who are meretricissimae. And for this it is that thou art pointed at with the finger as it were. {Jer 2:34-35}
paragraphs.anchor: Therefore also hast thou taught the wicked ones thy way.

paragraphs.text: In the skirts of thy garments. Heb., In thy wings - an allusion, say some, to birds of prey, which stain their wings with the blood of lesser fowls.
paragraphs.anchor: Also in thy skirts.

paragraphs.text: The life blood of innocent poor ones, of prophets especially. {Jer 2:30}
paragraphs.anchor: Is the blood of the souls.

paragraphs.text: Non in suffosione, as Calvin rendereth it, as an allusion to Exo 22:2.
paragraphs.anchor: I have not found it by secret search.

paragraphs.text: That is, In propatulo, in public view. Or, Super haec omnia, because they told thee of thy faults.
paragraphs.anchor: But upon all these.

paragraphs.text: Antiquum obtines; thou standest still upon thy justification. This doubleth thy fault. Homo agnoscit, Deus ignoseit. The best way is to plead guilty: confess, and go free.
paragraphs.anchor: Yet thou sayest, Because I am innocent.

paragraphs.text: Why gaddest thou {a} about so much to change thy way?] Or, Changing thy way; as hoping some way to mend thyself. Keep home, and trust God; go further, and fare worse. Creatures were never true to those that trusted them.
{a} Cur cursitas?
Or, From hence, into captivity.
paragraphs.anchor: Yea, thou shalt go from him.

paragraphs.text: Lamenting, as did Tamar. {2Sa 13:19}
paragraphs.anchor: With thine hands.

paragraphs.text: Where the beginning is carnal confidence, the end is shame, of any business, even of this life.
paragraphs.anchor: For the Lord hath rejected thy confidence.
